how-many-clients-does-booth-rent-need.ht.text:
BOOTH RENT VS COMMISSION CALCULATOR

How many clients do I need before booth rent pays off?

Booth rent keeps the full price of every ticket, but it also adds a fixed rent check, card fees, backbar, and often unpaid laundry and booking hours a salon used to absorb. At a light book, those fixed costs can cost more than commission would have taken. At a full book, the math flips, because rent stays fixed while commission keeps taking its cut of every new client. There is a specific client count where one flips into the other — this calculator solves for it as breakEvenClients.

The default book

On the calculator's defaults — $85 average ticket, 50% commission, a $275/week booth rent, 2.9% card fees, 10% backbar, and the other default costs — the break-even is about 8.4 clients a week. At the default 14 clients a week, that book is already past it: commission pays $603/week, booth rent pays $779.17, a $176.17-a-week ($8,808.50/year) edge for booth rent, and booth rent also wins on dollars per hour ($31.80 vs $30.92).

At 6 clients a week the same lease is $76.11 behind for the week, and needs about 2.4 more clients — roughly 8.4 total — to catch up. Below break-even, growing the book still helps both sides; it just helps booth rent faster, because commission only ever keeps half of each new ticket while booth rent keeps nearly all of it after fixed costs.

How high the rent can go

The same default 14-client book supports booth rent up to about $451.17 a week — not just the $275 in the example — before it stops beating the commission split. A salon offering a rent between the two is still worth checking client-by-client; a rent above the ceiling loses money against commission no matter how full the book is.

Open the calculator and enter your own ticket, client count, and costs — the breakeven, the extra clients needed, and the rent ceiling all update from your numbers, not these defaults.

What this is not

  • Not a claim that a bigger check is always the better job — see the hourly figures too; booth rent's unpaid hours can erase its dollar lead.
  • Not tax, insurance, or licensing advice for going independent.
  • Not a guarantee your actual client count or costs will hold — these are the numbers you type, not a forecast.

Common questions

How many clients do I need before booth rent pays off?

On the calculator's defaults — an $85 average ticket, a $275/week booth rent, 50% commission split, and the other default costs — booth rent breaks even at about 8.4 clients a week. Below that, the commission chair pays more; above it, booth rent pays more, and the gap grows with every extra client because booth rent keeps the full ticket price minus fixed costs, while commission only ever pays half.

What if I only see 6 clients a week?

On the same defaults, 6 clients a week puts commission $76.11 ahead for the week ($263 vs $186.89), and you would need about 2.4 more clients a week — roughly 8.4 total — before booth rent catches up. Below breakeven, more clients help both sides, but they help booth rent more, which is why the gap closes rather than staying fixed.

How high can the rent go before it stops paying?

On the default 14-clients-a-week book, booth rent could rise to about $451.17 a week — not just the $275 in the example — before it stops beating the same commission split. That gap between an offered rent and this ceiling is exactly what the calculator's own rent-offer field scores for you.

Does hourly pay flip at the same client count as weekly pay?

Not necessarily. This calculator scores both separately because they can disagree: booth rent usually adds unpaid hours a commission chair doesn't carry (laundry, booking, backbar prep), so a client count where booth rent wins on the week's total dollars can still lose on dollars per hour if those extra hours outweigh the extra take-home. Check both numbers, not just one.

index.html.text:
FOR STYLISTS, BARBERS, AND NAIL TECHS

Compare the hour, not just the check.

Booth rent keeps more of every ticket. It also adds rent, card fees, backbar, and the unpaid hours the salon used to cover. Enter your book once and see which deal actually pays you more — in dollars and per hour.

How many clients do I need before booth rent pays off? · This calculator vs. Vagaro · This calculator vs. guessing which pays more

Your book

Use a typical recent week, not your best Saturday. Retail stays put when the break-even client count is solved — new appointments do not automatically sell more product.

Commission deal

What the salon pays you. They typically cover rent, card fees, and laundry.

Booth-rent deal

You keep the ticket and pay the chair. Backbar is color and product used on clients, not retail you sell.

Payroll tax

On commission you are a W-2 employee and the salon pays half your FICA. On booth rent you are self-employed and pay both halves — an effective 14.1% of net against 7.65% of wages, charged to the booth side only. Until that comes out, the two checks are not the same dollars.

The bracket is optional: half of self-employment tax is deductible against income tax, and naming your bracket credits that back. Left at 0 it is worth nothing here, which understates booth rent rather than overstating it. Social Security stops at the wage base and Medicare does not; the default is the 2025 amount, indexed every January, so check yours if your chair income is near it. Income tax itself is not modelled — it lands on either deal much the same and depends on your whole household.

Common questions

How do I know if booth rent is worth it?

Look at both numbers. A bigger weekly check that costs six extra unpaid hours can be a worse job. If the hourly rate drops, you are paying for the lease with time you used to get paid for.

How many clients do I need to cover booth rent?

The break-even count is weekly appointments at your average ticket that make booth take-home match your current split, holding retail constant. Stay below it and the chair costs more than the extra you keep of each service.

What costs do stylists forget?

Card processing, color used on clients, wholesale cost of retail, booth insurance, towels, and the booking and laundry hours the front desk used to do.

What weekly rent would make booth rent match my commission split?

On the default book here (14 clients/week at $85, 50% commission, standard card and backbar rates), booth rent matches commission's $603 weekly take-home at $451.17/week in rent — well above the $275/week entered. Above that number the lease is taking more than the split ever did; the calculator's "Max weekly rent to match split" updates for your own numbers.

How many clients per week do I need before booth rent pays off?

The break-even is wherever booth take-home first matches commission at the same ticket and retail. On the default book that lands around 8.4 clients/week — the entered 14/week is already past it, which is why "Extra clients to match" reads zero. Below break-even, commission's smaller cut of a smaller check still beats rent, fees, and backbar.

Can adding more clients always make booth rent win?

No. Each extra client only helps booth rent if what you keep per ticket after card fees, backbar, and the salon's own commission rate is still positive. At a 92% commission split, for instance, card fees and backbar alone push that past 100% — every added client helps commission by at least as much, so no amount of volume closes the gap. When that happens the calculator reports "volume cannot close this gap"; the fix is a lower rent or lower backbar, not more chair time.

Do I pay more tax on booth rent than on commission?

Yes, and it is the most commonly missed number in this decision. On commission you are a W-2 employee: you pay the employee half of FICA, 7.65%, and the salon pays the matching half. On booth rent you are self-employed and pay both halves — 15.3%, charged on 92.35% of your net after rent, fees, and backbar. Nothing about the ticket changes; the same money is simply taxed about 6.5 points harder because of which deal you took (15.3% of 92.35% of net works out to an effective 14.1%, against the employee's 7.65%). On the default book that is roughly $3,200 a year, and it is why the max rent you can pay and still match your split is about $45 a week lower than the untaxed arithmetic suggests. Half of self-employment tax is deductible against income tax, which gives some of it back at your marginal rate; enter your bracket to count it.

Why might booth rent win on the weekly check but lose per hour?

Booth rent shifts laundry, booking, and restocking onto you, and those hours are unpaid on both sides but usually more of them on booth. On the default book, raising unpaid booth hours from 7 to 15 (no front desk covering that work) still leaves booth $176/week ahead in dollars — $779 vs commission's $603 — but its hourly rate falls to $23.97 against commission's $30.92. A bigger check spread over more unpaid hours can be the worse-paying job even while it wins on the total.

vs-guessing-which-pays-more.html.text:
← Booth Rent vs Commission Calculator

This calculator vs. guessing which pays more

Most stylists weigh a booth-rent offer the way it's pitched to them: roughly half the ticket to the salon, or a flat rent check. This page is about what changes when card fees, backbar, the retail split, and the unpaid hours each path adds are counted instead of eyeballed.

What each approach is

Guessing at the chair means comparing two round numbers in your head: "the salon keeps about half" against "the rent is $275 a week" -- without separating retail from service, without counting card fees or backbar product against the booth side, and without weighing either path's unpaid hours. It costs nothing and takes no time, which is exactly why it's the default most stylists run before ever opening a calculator.

This calculator takes the same book -- average ticket, clients per week, retail sales, and either a commission split or a booth-rent lease with its own card fees, backbar, retail cost, and other weekly cost -- and computes weekly, monthly, and annual take-home under each path, the take-home per hour once unpaid laundry and booking time is counted, the break-even client count, and the maximum rent that still matches the current split. Nothing is guessed; every figure comes from the numbers entered.

The gap is not rounding error. On this calculator's own shipped example -- an $85 average ticket, 14 clients a week, $80 a week in retail, a 50% service commission with a 10% retail commission, and a $275 weekly booth rent -- the napkin guess puts booth take-home at $995 a week (gross minus rent alone) against commission's $635 (half of everything, retail included), a $360 gap favoring booth. Run through this calculator, booth's real take-home is $779.17 once $36.83 in card fees, $119 in backbar, $40 in retail cost, and $20 in other weekly cost are counted, and commission's real take-home is $603 once retail is split at its own 10% rather than the 50% service rate. The real gap is $176.17 a week -- $183.83 narrower than the napkin math showed.

Per hour, the picture changes again. Booth rent's extra take-home comes with 5 more unpaid hours a week than commission on this example -- 24.5 hours against 19.5, once laundry, booking, and backbar prep are counted. Divide take-home by hours actually worked and commission pays $30.92 an hour, booth pays $31.80 -- an $0.88-an-hour edge, not the $360-a-week gap the napkin guess implies.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want an answer in ten seconds and I'm not touching my card-fee or backbar numbers right now.The chair-side napkin guess — free, but built from habit, not this book's own costs.
What does my own book actually pay under each path, with card fees, backbar, and retail split counted?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account, no upload.
Is the weekly dollar gap the whole story?No — check the per-hour figure too. On the shipped example it cuts a $360 napkin gap to $0.88 an hour.
How many clients do I need before booth rent pays off?This calculator's own break-even walkthrough.
Do I need an account, a spreadsheet, or a bookkeeper to use it?No, for either approach — the napkin guess needs nothing and neither does this calculator.

The napkin guess isn't a bad habit so much as a shortcut with a real cost that stays invisible until the rent check or the tax bill makes it obvious. This calculator doesn't remove the shortcut's convenience -- it's still one page, still free, still nothing to sign into -- it just replaces the two recalled numbers with the ones computed from your own book.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. This page names no company and compares against a napkin-math habit, not a product.

Common questions

Why not just compare the split to the rent in my head?

Because the two numbers a chair-side napkin check compares -- roughly half the ticket to the salon, or a flat rent check -- are not what either path actually pays. The napkin commission guess applies the service split to the whole book, including retail, which is usually commissioned at a lower rate. The napkin booth guess treats rent as the only cost, leaving out card processing, backbar product, the wholesale cost of retail sold, and other weekly expenses. Neither guess counts the unpaid hours -- laundry, booking, backbar prep -- that booth rent usually adds and a commission chair usually does not.

How much difference does it actually make?

On this calculator's own shipped example -- an $85 average ticket, 14 clients a week, $80 a week in retail, a 50% service commission with a 10% retail commission, and a $275 weekly booth rent with its card fees, backbar, and other costs -- the napkin guess is booth $995 a week (gross minus rent) against commission $635 a week (half of everything), a $360 gap favoring booth. The real numbers, once card fees, backbar, retail cost, and the smaller retail commission are counted, are booth $779.17 against commission $603, a $176.17 gap -- less than half of what the napkin math showed.

What does the napkin math miss on the hourly number?

The hours. On the shipped example, booth rent's extra take-home comes with 5 more unpaid hours a week than commission -- 24.5 hours against 19.5 -- for laundry, booking, and backbar prep a salon used to absorb. Once take-home is divided by hours actually worked, commission pays $30.92 an hour and booth pays $31.80: a $0.88-an-hour edge, not the $360-a-week gap the napkin guess implies. A stylist deciding on the dollar figure alone and one deciding on the hourly figure can reach different answers from the same book.

Is this the same as asking another stylist what they're on?

No. Another stylist's split or rent was set against their own ticket average, client count, retail sales, and costs -- borrowing their number and applying it to a different book is a second kind of guess, not a measurement of this one. This calculator takes one stylist's own numbers -- their ticket, their clients, their rent offer, their costs -- and computes both paths from that book, rather than from what someone else's chair happens to pay.

What if I don't know my exact card fee or backbar cost yet?

A rough estimate from a recent statement or product order is still far better than skipping straight to the napkin split, because card fees, backbar, and retail cost are exactly the costs the napkin guess leaves at zero. Starting from an estimate and refining it later is still a computed number checked against this book, rather than a round split recalled from habit.

vs-vagaro.html.text:
← Booth Rent vs Commission Calculator

This calculator vs. Vagaro

Two different shapes: Vagaro runs a whole salon, spa, or barbershop's booking, payments, and staff schedule as an ongoing subscription account, bought by the business. This page is a free, private worksheet for one stylist's own question — commission or booth rent, on their own book — before they sign a lease.

What each tool is for

Vagaro is salon, spa, and barbershop business-management software, sold under an ongoing subscription account to the business, not to an individual stylist. It runs an online booking page clients reserve appointments from directly, takes payments and processes card fees at checkout, schedules staff and chairs across a shop, sends marketing and appointment-reminder messages, and can track retail inventory, all synced across owners, employees, and booth renters on one account. Setting it up means creating a business account, building a service and booking calendar, and connecting payment processing — not a one-off comparison. Vagaro's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, feature tiers, or pricing, so only its well-documented category and identity are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not take bookings, process payments, or schedule staff. It takes one stylist's own book — average ticket, clients per week, retail, working weeks, and minutes per service — alongside either a commission split or a booth-rent lease with its rent, card fees, backbar, and other weekly cost, and works out weekly, monthly, and annual take-home under each path, the take-home per hour once unpaid laundry and booking time is counted, the break-even client count, the maximum rent that still matches the current split, and how payroll tax — employee FICA against self-employment tax — changes the answer. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and nothing typed in is uploaded.
